title: Brown Men and Women
subtitle: or, The South Sea Islands in 1895 and 1896
summary: Edward Reeves, a New Zealander and the author of “Homeward Bound after Thirty Years,” describes two voyages from Auckland on Union Steamship Company steamers: in July and August 1895 to Tonga, Samoa, and Fiji, and in July 1896 to the Cook Islands and the Society Islands, Tahiti among them. The book opens with Bully Hayes and memories of the New Zealand goldfields and with passengers’ yarns told at sea. It covers Tongan laws, land, and statistics; kava, marriage customs, and music, with seven tunes in notation; Stevenson’s house in Samoa; the queen of Rarotonga; and French rule in Tahiti. The last chapter is a sharp criticism of the rival missions in Tonga. Its descriptions of islanders, and especially of island women, are those of its time.

notes_on_text: Pages 77–78 and 133–136 are missing from the scan used (University of Toronto) and are taken from another copy at the Internet Archive (University of California).
The map of Tongatabu, which the title page and the text announce as the frontispiece of Chapter III, is in none of the scans at the Internet Archive and is missing here.
The seven tunes on pp. 133–136 and elsewhere are given as pictures of the printed music.
A corner of p. 17 is torn away in the scan used; the lost words were read from the University of California copy.
Quoted passages printed in smaller type, among them most of the yarns of Chapter II, are set off as quotations.

“Excerpts from Tongan Official Documents” is printed in small type along the foot of pp. 268–286, under the text of Chapter X, as a second, separate text; the author calls it “a concurrent and correlative substatement”. Here it follows Chapter X as a section of its own, with the printed page numbers. The small raised numbers in Chapter X refer to the numbers in parentheses in these excerpts.
Tables that belong to footnotes on pp. 25 and 111 follow the text of their page.
Two footnotes printed in two paragraphs (pp. 30 and 289) are given as one paragraph each.

The two tables printed in footnotes (pp. 25 and 111) are given as one line of the note, the headings first and the rows separated by semicolons; the note to “Niua Tobutabu” in the second table follows it in the same note, after its asterisk. The paragraph that resumes after the printed music (p. 137) begins a new paragraph.
